items.stem: A compliance rule says a summary must never contain a card number. The prototype relies on one prompt line asking the model to omit them. What should the spec say about this rule?

options.a: Keep the prompt line and add a second line that repeats the request more firmly
options.b: Measure how often the model leaks a number and accept a low enough rate
options.c: Move the instruction to the start so the model weighs it more heavily
options.d: Enforce it with a pattern check in code, and test it with planted tickets

items.explanation: A guarantee that must always hold belongs in code; a prompt line is only a request to the model, so the spec names which rules need the guarantee.

items.stem: A drafting feature takes nine seconds to deliver its whole answer, and the team wants it faster without changing the model tier. Which first step does the page rank highest?

options.a: Chain a second call that rewrites the draft more briefly than the first
options.b: Ask for a shorter output, since producing tokens dominates the wait
options.c: Buy a higher usage plan so that each single call finishes sooner
options.d: Stream the reply, which shortens the total time until it is complete

items.explanation: Output length is the largest part of the wait. A higher tier does not make one call finish sooner, and streaming does not shorten the total time.

items.stem: Alerts at a retail firm show a sharp rise in 400 responses right after a release. What does the page say this pattern indicates?

options.a: A defect in what the client code sends
options.b: A capacity shortage that a higher tier would relieve
options.c: A fault inside the provider that will clear unaided
options.d: A burst that emptied the organisation's token bucket

items.explanation: A rise in 429s is a capacity story, a rise in 400s usually points at your requests (or at a spend limit you set, which also returns a 400), and a rise in 5xx is a provider story. Right after a release, the requests the new code sends are the first place to look.

items.stem: A team moves its summary feature to claude-sonnet-5-5 and keeps a call that sets temperature to 0.3. What does the page predict for those calls?

options.a: They run unchanged, because sampling settings are honoured on every model
options.b: They run but with the value ignored, so the output stays the same
options.c: They are refused with a 400 error, because non-default sampling values are rejected
options.d: They are refused with a 429 error until the setting is removed

items.explanation: The sampling parameters temperature, top_p and top_k are rejected with a 400 error on Sonnet 5.5 for any non-default value, so the call must change.

items.stem: A hand-written client crashes with a JSON decode error on a failed call, although the API documents that its errors are JSON. Which explanation fits?

options.a: The service sometimes sends plain text instead of JSON, but only for 5xx statuses
options.b: An intermediary on the route sent back an HTML page instead of the service
options.c: The version header was wrong, which silently switches the format of every error body
options.d: The error type was new to the client, which forces a non-JSON reply

items.explanation: The promise covers the API's own errors; a proxy or edge in front of it can answer with a page that is not JSON, and retrying gets the same page.

items.stem: A team assumes the SDK restricts how many requests run at once because it ships with sensible defaults. What does the page say about this?

options.a: It queues anything beyond ten simultaneous calls by default
options.b: It spaces calls out whenever a retry is pending for an earlier one, from the outset
options.c: Nothing in it caps parallelism, so the application must add that limit
options.d: It limits parallelism only for streamed replies that share a pool

items.explanation: The SDK does not bound concurrency: fifty parallel calls are fifty parallel calls, so the application adds the bound (module 16).

items.stem: A nightly job sets a very large max_tokens on a non-streaming call for a long report, and calls sometimes die after several minutes with no response. Which fix does the page give?

options.a: Raise the SDK timeout beyond ten minutes so the wait can complete
options.b: Lower the retry count so that failed attempts stop piling up
options.c: Reopen the link as a websocket so that either side may speak at any time
options.d: Receive incremental events so the link is never idle, or poll a batch for results

items.explanation: Networks may drop idle connections; incremental events keep bytes flowing, and a batch can be polled instead of holding a connection open.

items.stem: After a rollout, users behind a corporate proxy see streamed text arrive in one lump at the end. What does the page say describes this?

options.a: A device on the path is buffering the response
options.b: The stream was swapped for a websocket, whose frames are grouped by design
options.c: The model wrote everything first, because streaming only changes the format
options.d: The SDK holds every event back until the usage figures are known

items.explanation: A proxy that buffers responses turns a stream into one lump and defeats its purpose.

items.stem: A developer stores only the text of each assistant reply in a database and rebuilds the history from it. After enabling thinking with tools, requests start returning a 400. What does the page say causes it?

options.a: The assistant turns should have been sent under the system role instead
options.b: Reasoning blocks were dropped, and they must go back exactly as received
options.c: Text-only storage doubles the token count, which breaches the context limit
options.d: Thinking cannot be combined with any history that is longer than one turn

items.explanation: If the latest assistant message holds thinking blocks, editing or dropping them returns a 400; the content list is stored as received.

items.stem: A call that reuses a 200,000-token cached document and asks a 50-token question reports input_tokens of 50. A cost dashboard sums only that number. What does it understate?

options.a: The full volume sent, since prefixes read earlier or stored now sit in separate fields
options.b: The output volume, which grows whenever the document in use is a long one
options.c: The count of calls made, since cached ones are left out of the total tally
options.d: Nothing, because that field already reports everything the call consumed

items.explanation: input_tokens counts only what follows the last breakpoint; the total is cache reads plus cache creation plus input_tokens (here 200,050).

items.stem: A reply arrives with status 200, stop_reason max_tokens and a half-written JSON object. What should the client do?

options.a: Parse it leniently, since a 200 status means the answer is complete
options.b: Append the half-written text as an assistant turn and call again
options.c: Add a stop sequence so that the text ends at the closing brace
options.d: Mark it as cut, then retry with a higher ceiling

items.explanation: A max_tokens reply stops where it stands, so the JSON is incomplete; check stop_reason before parsing. Ending the list with the cut text is a prefill, which returns a 400.

items.stem: A client appends the user's turn to its history, then the call times out. The retry sends two user turns in a row, a different conversation from the one the user saw. Which rule prevents this?

options.a: Retry with a longer timeout and leave the history exactly as it stands
options.b: Store the conversation on the server so that the API remembers the earlier turns
options.c: Hold the new message back from the record until the exchange has fully succeeded
options.d: Send the unanswered message twice so that the retry cannot lose it

items.explanation: Commit a turn only when the whole exchange succeeded: on any failure, remove the user turn before the error leaves the function.

items.stem: At the end of the billing cycle, every call returns a 429 of type rate_limit_error that carries no retry-after header, and the SDK's retries all fail. The error code reads enforced_spend_limit_reached. What is the first action?

options.a: Add jitter to the retry delays so that the clients spread out over the hour
options.b: Switch to a cheaper model so that the same traffic fits inside the quota
options.c: Raise max_retries so that later attempts get through once capacity returns
options.d: Lift the organisation's monthly cap, since access stays paused until it resumes

items.explanation: A spend cap pauses usage until the next month, has no retry-after, and the SDK's retries do not know it; a person must act.

items.stem: A streamed reply opens with a 200, and later a fault is announced in the middle of it. How should the client treat the exchange?

options.a: As a success, keeping the partial text because that code was already sent
options.b: As a 4xx or 5xx case, using the usual branch that is keyed on the status
options.c: As failed, whatever the initial code said
options.d: As a transient glitch, resending at once without reading the rest of the stream

items.explanation: Streaming adds an error that no status can express; the client reads the stream to its end and treats an error event or a missing message_stop as a failure.

items.stem: A tool that files a support ticket runs inside a call that is retried. The first attempt had succeeded on the server before the timeout. How is a duplicate ticket avoided?

options.a: Give the action its own unique key, checked before acting
options.b: Tell the model in the prompt never to file the same ticket twice
options.c: Pass the SDK's idempotency parameter on the message creation request
options.d: Disable retries for the whole application and accept the failure rate

items.explanation: The Messages API documents no idempotency key, so the key is your design: check it before acting and store the result under it. Retry the call, never the side effect.

items.stem: An interactive screen keeps the SDK defaults of a ten-minute timeout and two retries, and a connection hangs. How long can the user wait before seeing an error?

options.a: About ten minutes, since only the first attempt is allowed to wait that long
options.b: About half an hour
options.c: About a second and a half, which is the length of the back-off alone
options.d: About two minutes, because the retries share a single clock between them

items.explanation: Worst case is attempts times timeout plus the waits: three attempts of ten minutes, so thirty minutes. Set a total deadline from the latency budget.

items.stem: A job must send 600 requests a minute, and each call takes about 6 seconds to finish. What bound on calls in flight fits?

options.a: About ten, since that is how many are started during each second
options.b: About six hundred, so that the whole minute's work can be waiting together
options.c: About sixty
options.d: About six, matching the time that each one needs to complete

items.explanation: Little's law: requests in flight equal the rate times the duration, so 10 a second times 6 seconds is about 60.

items.stem: An async web endpoint uses the synchronous client, and while one visitor's reply is awaited, no other visitor is served. Why?

options.a: Nothing hands control back during the pause, so the single thread is held
options.b: The synchronous client opens a fresh connection pool for each visitor
options.c: Every visitor shares one rate limit, and the first request consumes all of it
options.d: The server runs tasks in parallel only when the replies are streamed

items.explanation: A call that waits without yielding stops the event loop, and every other task waits with it; use the async client inside async code.

items.stem: A job reads a million-line file into a list and then hands items to a bounded pool. The tests pass, but production runs out of memory. Which property is missing?

options.a: A larger limit on workers so that the list drains faster, at least by default
options.b: Pulling from the source only when a worker has room for more
options.c: A retry loop around each worker's call to the model
options.d: A client-side token bucket sized from the request limit

items.explanation: Backpressure means taking the next item only when there is room for it; copying the input first passes every other test and fails the lazy-pull case.

items.stem: A client sums the output_tokens of every message_delta in a stream, and its cost report is several times too high. What is the mistake?

options.a: Only the first of these events carries counts, and the rest repeat it
options.b: Output counts belong to the opening event, which the client skipped
options.c: The ping events were counted too, and each of them adds a small amount
options.d: Each such event restates the running total, so the stored figure should be replaced

items.explanation: The output count in message_delta is cumulative: replace the stored one, do not add to it.

items.stem: A developer parses each partial_json fragment as it arrives and gets exceptions on most of them. What is the fix?

options.a: Request smaller deltas by lowering the token ceiling of the call
options.b: Skip every fragment that fails and keep only the valid objects
options.c: Concatenate the pieces and decode once, after the block ends
options.d: Ask the model to emit complete objects by adding a stop sequence

items.explanation: The fragments of a tool input are text that is not valid JSON until the block ends; join them and parse once.

items.stem: A nightly job classifies short texts into labels with no one waiting, and a colleague proposes streaming everything for safety. What does the page say?

options.a: Streaming lowers the per-token price, so it pays off at volume
options.b: Streamed calls count against separate and higher limits
options.c: Streaming is required whenever an answer may run past a few hundred tokens
options.d: The plain call is simpler and has fewer ways to fail here

items.explanation: Streaming changes when bytes arrive, not what tokens cost or what limits allow; with no waiting person, no very long answer and no idle-dropping proxy, the plain call is simpler.

items.stem: A newer model lists a price 20 percent below its predecessor's per token, but its tokenizer yields about 30 percent more tokens for the same text. What happens to the cost of a task?

options.a: It runs slightly dearer, near 1.04 times the earlier one
options.b: It falls by 20 percent, since the listed price decides the outcome
options.c: It falls by about half, because both changes favour the buyer
options.d: It stays identical, because the two changes cancel each other exactly

items.explanation: Cost per task is 0.8 times 1.3, which is 1.04: compare on a sample, not per million tokens.

items.stem: A team with no evaluation history must pick a model for a new feature. Which method does the page describe?

options.a: Start with the cheapest and move up only after customers complain
options.b: Start with a capable one, measure on real cases, then step down while quality holds
options.c: Pick the newest release, since later versions are always the cheaper ones
options.d: Choose the largest available and keep it, because quality is the first concern in everyday use

items.explanation: Begin capable so a failure means the task is hard, then move down a tier at a time and keep the last tier that held.

items.stem: A team wants to refuse oversized inputs before any paid call and considers the token counting endpoint. What does the page say about it?

options.a: It returns the exact billed amount, including output and thinking tokens
options.b: It costs nothing and gives an estimate, with limits of its own
options.c: It shares one rate limit with message creation, so the two compete
options.d: It accepts every input the Messages API accepts, including server tools

items.explanation: Counting is free, an estimate, separately rate limited, and rejects some inputs such as server tools; exact figures come from usage afterwards.

items.stem: After a one-line change of model id to claude-opus-5-5, every request fails with a 400, and the logs show a manual thinking budget and a temperature of 0.3 in the body. What is the cause and cure?

options.a: The alias moved silently, so the id should be pinned to a dated snapshot
options.b: The tokenizer changed, so max_tokens must be doubled for every call
options.c: The retirement date has passed, so the old id returns errors for all callers in everyday use
options.d: The newer release refuses those settings, so the builder must adapt to each target

items.explanation: Opus 5.5 rejects manual thinking budgets and non-default sampling values with a 400; change the request builder together with the id.

items.stem: A reply to a thinking call shows a 250-token answer, while usage reports output_tokens of 1,900. How many tokens are billed?

options.a: Only the 250 shown, since the hidden part is free
options.b: The 250 shown plus a flat fee for each reasoning block
options.c: All 1,900, since hidden reasoning is charged at the generation rate
options.d: Only the 1,650 reasoning tokens, since answer text is billed with the input

items.explanation: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens: you pay for the full process, and output_tokens is the total billed.

items.stem: Midway through a tool loop, the application switches the thinking mode. What does the API do?

options.a: It quietly drops reasoning for that request
options.b: It returns a 400 error that names the unsupported change
options.c: It applies the new mode starting from the next turn
options.d: It restarts the loop from the first tool call

items.explanation: The API does not error: it silently disables thinking for that request. Toggle between turns, not within them.

items.stem: Midway through a long conversation that uses a prompt cache, the application raises effort at the top level. What follows?

options.a: Nothing, since effort is a soft signal outside the cached content itself
options.b: The tool definitions are invalidated, while messages stay valid
options.c: The saving is kept, because effort is not a thinking parameter
options.d: Earlier messages must be written afresh, as the setting is baked into the prefix

items.explanation: Changing thinking or effort discards the cached messages because the resolved configuration is rendered into the prompt.

items.stem: Every request carries a large static system prompt followed by one block holding a timestamp and the user's question, with the cache marker on that last block. Usage shows a write on every call and no reads. What fixes it?

options.a: Move the breakpoint up to the final section that never changes
options.b: Raise the lifetime to one hour so the entry outlasts the changing text
options.c: Add a second marker on the question so that both parts are stored
options.d: Switch on automatic caching, which skips any content that varies

items.explanation: A marker on a block that varies makes the hash differ every time; move it to the last stable block, because the lookback only finds entries written at earlier breakpoints.

items.stem: A system prompt of about 300 tokens on claude-sonnet-5-5 is marked for caching, yet both cache fields read 0 and no error appears. Why?

options.a: The model needs 4,096 tokens, so the prefix was far too short to qualify
options.b: Entries are only written once a second request repeats the same prefix
options.c: The prefix is under the 512 minimum, so nothing is stored and nothing warns you
options.d: An error was raised, but the SDK hides it unless verbose logging is turned up on most systems

items.explanation: A prefix shorter than the model's minimum is processed without caching and no error is returned; check for the two zeros in usage.

items.stem: A prefix is reused about once a minute all day. Which lifetime does the page favour?

options.a: The one-hour one, because its write is cheaper than the short one's write
options.b: The default short one, because every hit extends it at no added cost
options.c: The one-hour one, since a short entry otherwise lapses after a single minute
options.d: Neither, since an entry refreshes only after the response has been completed

items.explanation: A prompt used more often than every five minutes keeps its five-minute entry alive for free; the one-hour write costs 2 times base and needs a third request to pay back.

items.stem: A nightly job has 150,000 short prompts totalling about 40 MB. How many batches does it need at the least?

options.a: One, since the 256 MB ceiling is nowhere near reached by this job in everyday use
options.b: Two, because the count cap of 100,000 is reached before the size cap
options.c: Three, because every batch may hold at most 50,000 entries
options.d: Six, since each batch is limited to 25,000 entries of any size

items.explanation: A batch holds 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever is reached first; 150,000 requests exceed the count limit although the size is small.

items.stem: A batch includes a body copied from a live path that sets stream to true. When does the refusal surface?

options.a: Immediately, when the submission returns a 400 error
options.b: Never, because the flag is silently ignored in bulk jobs, from the outset
options.c: Only with the results, once processing of all entries has ended
options.d: At the first poll, when the status changes to canceling

items.explanation: Validation of each request's params runs asynchronously, and validation errors are returned when processing of the entire batch has ended.

items.stem: A batch ends with 700 succeeded, 200 errored and 100 expired results. What is billed?

options.a: Only the completed ones, at half the standard price
options.b: All 1,000, since expired entries had already been reserved
options.c: The completed and the errored, since an error still used compute
options.d: The 700 at full price, with the 200 errors at half

items.explanation: You are not billed for errored, canceled or expired requests; usage on the rest is charged at 50 percent of standard prices.

items.stem: A team sends a direct-API call to Google Cloud without changes, and it is rejected. What must differ?

options.a: The model name needs an anthropic. prefix, and the version stays in a header, from the outset
options.b: The version header is dropped, and the model name stays where it was
options.c: Only the credential changes, since the body shape is identical everywhere
options.d: The model name goes into the endpoint path and the version moves into the payload

items.explanation: On Google Cloud the model is specified in the endpoint URL and anthropic_version is passed in the body, set to vertex-2023-10-16.

items.stem: A team on Amazon Bedrock plans a nightly job through the Message Batches API for half-price processing. What does the page say?

options.a: It is supported, but only through regional endpoints at a 10 percent premium
options.b: The integration offers no such endpoint, so that reduced rate cannot be had
options.c: It is supported, with a reduction of 25 percent in place of the usual half
options.d: It is supported on both clouds, though with a smaller maximum batch size

items.explanation: Bedrock lists the Message Batches API among its unsupported endpoints, so the discount that belongs to it is unavailable there.

items.stem: A compliance rule demands that traffic is guaranteed to pass only through named geographic regions on Google Cloud. What does the page say about the price against the dynamic option?

options.a: No difference, since every endpoint kind shares one rate
options.b: A discount of 10 percent, since traffic is spread over fewer areas
options.c: Double the rate, since guaranteed routing needs reserved capacity
options.d: A premium of 10 percent over what global routing charges

items.explanation: Regional and multi-region endpoints include a 10 percent pricing premium over global endpoints.

items.stem: A review finds an allow statement granting bedrock:* on * to an application's role. What change does the page require?

options.a: Keep the wildcard and add a Deny for every action that manages resources
options.b: Replace the action wildcard with a resource wildcard across all inference profiles
options.c: List the one invoke action and the one model ARN it needs
options.d: Switch to an administrator role that the cloud vendor already maintains

items.explanation: A policy adds what a job needs and nothing more: a named action on a specific model, since a wildcard grants every action on every model.

items.stem: A service account needs to do nothing except invoke a Claude endpoint on Google Cloud. Which grant fits?

options.a: A custom role that holds just the predict permission
options.b: The predefined user role, which is easy to assign and tightly scoped
options.c: A basic Editor role that is limited to the one project
options.d: A predefined role combined with a deny on the deploy permission

items.explanation: Predefined roles often contain more permissions than you need; a custom role with aiplatform.endpoints.predict lets the account call the endpoint but not control it.

items.stem: A Google Cloud project must keep data in Europe while calling claude-sonnet-5-5. Which setup fits?

options.a: A specific europe- region, which serves every current model
options.b: The global endpoint, which routes within Europe whenever capacity allows
options.c: Any endpoint, as the residency rule applies only to Bedrock
options.d: The multi-region eu endpoint, since a specific region serves only an older model

items.explanation: A specific region serves claude-sonnet-4-6 only, so Sonnet 5.5 in the EU uses the eu multi-region endpoint at the premium.

items.stem: A customer's message contains the literal characters {{question}}, and in the finished prompt those characters have been swapped for the application's own question text. What went wrong?

options.a: Filling ran repeatedly, so inserted data was read as part of the template
options.b: The customer text should have gone into the system prompt instead
options.c: The tags around the variable were not given a random identifier
options.d: The placeholder syntax must be changed from braces to angle brackets

items.explanation: A template is filled in one pass, left to right, and never rescanned, so a value that looks like a placeholder stays data.

items.stem: A prompt rule says only "never use ellipses", and the replies are read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, yet ellipses still slip through now and then. What does the page suggest?

options.a: Repeat the rule in capital letters at the top and again at the end
options.b: Add the reason, so the model generalises beyond the cases it names
options.c: Replace it with a list of conditionals for each situation that produces one
options.d: Move the rule into the user turn, where it will be read more carefully

items.explanation: A constraint with its reason works better than a bare one: Claude is smart enough to generalize from the explanation.

items.stem: A classifier prompt includes five examples that all end with the label billing, and the model now answers billing for almost everything. What fix does the page give?

options.a: Add five more examples, all of them with the same billing label
options.b: Replace the examples with the instruction to think step by step
options.c: Diversify: add a hard case, a no-match case and a misleading one
options.d: Move the examples below the question so the model attends to them less

items.explanation: Examples should be diverse: five that share one label teach "answer billing"; include a hard case, a no-match case and a case whose obvious reading is wrong.

items.stem: A structured-output call returns status 200 with stop_reason refusal, and the client crashes while parsing the body against the schema. What does the page say?

options.a: Retry the same request until a reply that follows the schema comes back, from the outset
options.b: Raise max_tokens, since a refusal is a reply that was cut short
options.c: Loosen the schema so that free text is accepted in every field
options.d: Safety messages override the format promise, so inspect why it ended first

items.explanation: On a refusal the output may not match the schema because the refusal message takes precedence; read stop_reason before the body and report it, do not repeat it.

items.stem: A schema sent with output_config.format carries minimum and maxLength limits on fields, and the call fails with a 400. What is the remedy?

options.a: Raise the compilation limit by splitting the schema across several strict tools
options.b: Drop them from the version the API sees, describe them in text, and verify replies in code
options.c: Set additionalProperties to true, which turns each constraint into a hint
options.d: Switch to forced tool choice, which accepts every JSON Schema keyword

items.explanation: Numerical and string constraints are unsupported and give a 400; helpers remove them, add them to the description, and a validating helper still enforces them in your code.

items.stem: An extractor's first reply fails validation on three fields. What should the follow-up request hold?

options.a: Only the original prompt, repeated so that the same attempt runs afresh
options.b: Only the first issue, so that each call fixes one thing at a time
options.c: The model's own earlier text and every issue named with its path
options.d: The original prompt plus a request to answer more carefully this time

items.explanation: Send the whole conversation: the first message, the reply as an assistant message, and a user message listing each problem with its path.

items.stem: To get reliably shaped JSON, a team sets tool_choice to a named function on claude-sonnet-5-5. What happens, and what does the page offer instead?

options.a: A 400 error comes back; auto selection with strict schemas gives the assurance
options.b: The call succeeds, and the model writes an explanation before the function call
options.c: The call succeeds, but the forced choice is dropped after the first request
options.d: A 429 comes back, since forced selection counts against a separate limit

items.explanation: On Sonnet 5.5, any and tool return a 400 error; use auto with strict tool use, or structured outputs for a fixed JSON shape.

items.stem: A loop adds a sentence reading Here are the results before the first tool_result in the user message. What follows?

options.a: Nothing breaks, though the sentence costs a few extra input tokens
options.b: The model reads the sentence as a helpful label and answers more quickly
options.c: A silent loss of parallel calls in later turns, with no error at all
options.d: A 400 error, because content blocks that answer calls must lead and prose must trail

items.explanation: The tool_result blocks must come first in the content array; any text must come after all of them, or the request returns a 400 error.

items.stem: A loop keyed only on stop_reason runs up cost because a confused model keeps invoking a function that keeps failing. What safeguard does the page add?

options.a: A longer description so the model stops calling the broken function in many setups
options.b: A retry with exponential back-off between each model request
options.c: A ceiling on iterations, with a distinct status reported when it is hit
options.d: A forced tool choice on every request so that the loop ends sooner

items.explanation: A loop keyed on stop_reason ends when the model decides to end it, so it needs its own limit of model calls and a status for reaching it.

items.stem: A loop replies to three simultaneous requests from the model with three separate user messages, one answer in each. What does the page predict?

options.a: Concurrent invocation fades, since that layout trains it toward single calls
options.b: Nothing changes, because answers are matched by identifier whatever the grouping
options.c: The API merges them into one message before the next model turn
options.d: Each later turn returns a 429 for exceeding the allowed message rate

items.explanation: Formatting results as a separate user message for each one teaches Claude to avoid parallel calls; return all results together in one user message.

items.stem: A team keeps a nine-hundred-line API reference in CLAUDE.md, and every session now feels slow and unfocused. What does the page recommend?

options.a: Split the document across several CLAUDE.md files so that each stays short
options.b: Relocate the material into a skill, whose body loads on demand
options.c: Convert the document into a hook that prints it at the start of each session
options.d: Add a subagent that reads the file and answers every question about it

items.explanation: CLAUDE.md loads in full on every request, so keep it under 200 lines and move reference material to skills, which load on demand.

items.stem: A rule never to touch the .env file sits in CLAUDE.md, yet Claude modified it in one session. What does the page advise for a rule that must hold?

options.a: Repeat the rule in a skill so that it is stated in two places
options.b: Add a hook before tool use that blocks the change, since triggers are guaranteed
options.c: Move the rule into an output style, which is enforced for the whole session, at least by default
options.d: Rephrase the rule in capital letters and explain why it matters

items.explanation: A sentence in CLAUDE.md is a request, not a guarantee; a PreToolUse hook that blocks the edit is enforcement.

items.stem: An investigation reads dozens of files, and the main conversation's context is filling up fast. Which feature fits best?

options.a: A skill, which loads the file contents into the main window when invoked
options.b: A larger CLAUDE.md that records what each file contains in detail
options.c: An MCP server that exposes every file to the model as a callable function
options.d: An isolated worker whose own window hands back only a summary

items.explanation: A subagent uses a separate window with its own tokens and returns only a summary, while a skill adds to the main window.

items.stem: Users search for the exact code E-4012, but a vector-only index ranks that page far down. What fits?

options.a: Add BM25 scoring, which matches literal strings, then merge both result lists
options.b: Raise the chunk size so that each page is embedded as a single piece
options.c: Add more overlap between neighbours so that the code is repeated around it
options.d: Switch to a larger embedding model that Anthropic offers for retrieval

items.explanation: An embedding is weaker with exact strings such as error codes, while BM25 finds them; the two indexes fail on different questions, so use both. Anthropic offers no embedding model.

items.stem: A reranker is given only the top five fused results, and the relevant chunk sits at rank twelve. What happens?

options.a: It is promoted to first, since the reranker scores the whole corpus
options.b: It moves up by seven places, the difference between the two ranks
options.c: It stays out of reach, because candidates beyond that group are never scored
options.d: It is found by the keyword index, which takes over once the reranker runs, at least by default

items.explanation: A reranker orders only the pool; a chunk outside it is never considered, so the pool must contain the answer and reranking cannot fix a retrieval that missed.

items.stem: A passage reading "revenue grew 3 percent over the previous quarter" names no company or period, and searches for one firm's results never surface it. What fix does Anthropic's write-up describe?

options.a: Use fewer words per window so that each carries a single number
options.b: Have a model add a situating sentence to each piece before indexing
options.c: Rely on a larger model for generation, since it will infer the company
options.d: Retrieve only five items so that vague ones are filtered out

items.explanation: Contextual retrieval prepends chunk-specific explanatory context to each chunk before embedding and before building the keyword index.

items.stem: A trimming routine removes the oldest messages one at a time, and the next request returns a 400 error. What is the likely cause?

options.a: The window shrank below the size of the output limit
options.b: Summaries stacked, leaving two of them in the conversation
options.c: Caching misses pushed the input over the window
options.d: A call to a function lost the answer that must follow it directly

items.explanation: A tool result must immediately follow its tool use; keeping one without the other fails with a 400, so drop whole turns.

items.stem: A team using compaction at a token threshold computes spend from top-level input_tokens and output_tokens, and invoices come out higher than its reports. Why?

options.a: Compaction doubles the price of every token that passes through it
options.b: Top-level counts show cached reads at full price, while billing discounts them in many setups
options.c: Those counters omit the condensing pass; the iterations list has the full figures
options.d: Summaries are billed to a separate workspace that the reports leave out

items.explanation: The top-level counts do not include compaction iteration usage; sum across the usage.iterations array to find what was billed.

items.stem: A team needs answers that point at their source passages and also fit a fixed JSON layout. Which design does the page suggest?

options.a: Split it: cite in one call and shape the result in another that carries no documents
options.b: Enable both in one call and let the API interleave pointers inside the schema, at least by default
options.c: Enable pointers on half of the documents and the schema on the rest
options.d: Put the layout in a system prompt, which the citation feature then enforces

items.explanation: Citations and structured outputs are incompatible and return a 400 error together; separate the two steps, or ask for an evidence field and check it in code.

items.stem: A support app accepts a file_id typed by the end user to attach an earlier upload to a request. What risk does the page name?

options.a: All stored items are shared workspace-wide, exposing one customer's data to another
options.b: Ids expire after an hour, so the attachment would then fail without any warning
options.c: The id can be downloaded back by anyone who happens to know it afterwards
options.d: Each reference doubles the stored size, which counts against the quota for storage

items.explanation: Uploaded files are accessible to the entire workspace, not scoped to an end user; never accept file_id values from end users.

items.stem: Claude returns a point on an image that the API shrank and then padded to a multiple of 28 on the bottom and right. To map it back, which size is the divisor?

options.a: The padded dimensions, since that is the picture the model processed
options.b: The reduced dimensions, since the added strip contains nothing
options.c: The original dimensions, since the point is already in that space
options.d: Either one, since the difference is under 28 pixels and negligible

items.explanation: Always normalize by the resized dimensions, not the padded ones: the padding sits on the bottom and right and holds no content.

items.stem: A request carrying 25 images, one of them 3000 pixels wide, is rejected with an error that mentions many-image requests. What remedy does the page give?

options.a: Switch the pictures to base64, which the stricter limit does not cover
options.b: Move the pictures after the text, since the order decides which limit applies
options.c: Shrink each picture so no side passes 2000 px, or send at most 20 blocks
options.d: Move to a model with a 1M window, which lifts the per-side cap

items.explanation: Above 20 images a stricter per-image dimension limit applies; resize so neither dimension exceeds 2000 px, or keep the request to 20 or fewer image and document blocks.

items.stem: A team sends PDFs through the Converse API on Amazon Bedrock and finds that Claude cannot discuss the charts inside them. What is the usual reason?

options.a: Charts are removed from every PDF before it is converted into page pictures, at least by default
options.b: Bedrock supports only PDFs whose pages hold no more than 600 words
options.c: The model reads PDFs by URL only, so base64 uploads drop the pictures
options.d: Without the citation setting, only plain text extraction is applied to pages

items.explanation: Without citations enabled, Converse falls back to basic text extraction, which is the usual reason charts seem to be missing.

items.stem: A computer-use reply holds four actions in order, and the early click fails. How must the loop answer?

options.a: Return an error for that step and the fixed skipped notice for every later step
options.b: Run the remaining actions anyway and report only the click's error
options.c: Answer only the first block, since the rest were never reached
options.d: Skip the failed action silently and answer the rest as normal

items.explanation: Run blocks in order and stop at the first failure: is_error with a description for the failed one and the fixed text "Not executed: an earlier computer action in this turn failed." for each later one.

items.stem: A loop returns reduced screenshots of a 2560 by 1440 display, and Claude answers with a click at 698, 73. What must the loop do before clicking?

options.a: Click exactly where Claude said, since the coordinates are in real pixel space
options.b: Multiply the numbers by the scale factor, since the picture was smaller
options.c: Resize the next picture back up to the full display before returning it
options.d: Divide by the applied scale factor and clamp the result to the physical panel

items.explanation: Coordinates are in the pixel space of the image Claude saw: if you scale screenshots down, scale Claude's coordinates back up before applying them, and clamp them into the screen.

items.stem: A computer-use loop asks a person to approve once at the start of a task, yet a reply completed a payment that nobody reviewed. What does the page require?

options.a: Another approval at the end of the task, once all actions have run
options.b: A check ahead of every risky block, since a single turn finishes several steps
options.c: A classifier setting, which makes confirmations unnecessary
options.d: A longer system prompt asking the model to avoid payment pages

items.explanation: A batch can complete a multistep action within one turn, so the check belongs before each block runs, not once per reply and not at the start.

items.stem: A long agent loop keeps every screenshot, and after a few dozen turns requests start failing on image size although each capture was accepted earlier. What does the page explain?

options.a: Screenshots expire from the Files API after an hour and must be re-uploaded
options.b: The toolset downsizes old captures by half each turn until they are rejected, as a rule of thumb
options.c: Beyond twenty pictures in a single call, a tighter per-side cap applies to each
options.d: Each capture's cost doubles after the tenth, which breaches the size cap

items.explanation: Once a request carries more than 20 images, every image in it is held to a stricter per-side limit; resize to 2000 px or prune.

items.stem: A team wants read-only schema information that the application itself chooses how to use, with no model decision involved. Which primitive fits?

options.a: A tool, because the model should discover and invoke it automatically on demand
options.b: A prompt, because a person picks it from a menu before each session starts
options.c: A sampling request, because the server should ask the client for that context
options.d: A resource, which the hosting program selects and consumes directly

items.explanation: Resources are passive, read-only data sources controlled by the application; tools are model-controlled and prompts are user-controlled.

items.stem: A Python server function raises a plain ValueError whose message explains what to fix, but the model never retries with a better value. Why?

options.a: Only ToolError carries its wording to the client; other exceptions are reported without it
options.b: ValueError is converted into a JSON-RPC protocol error that models are told to ignore in many setups
options.c: The SDK retries ValueError on the server, so the model never sees a failure at all
options.d: Messages longer than a single line are cut off before they reach the model

items.explanation: In the Python SDK, raise ToolError for an expected failure: the message of an exception that is not a ToolError is not shown to the client.

items.stem: A stdio server prints progress with print() and every client now fails to parse its messages. What is the fix?

options.a: Flush stdout after every print so that the lines are delivered whole
options.b: Direct diagnostics to a logger that writes to stderr
options.c: Prefix each printed line with a JSON-RPC version field to look valid
options.d: Run the server inside a container so that its output is kept isolated

items.explanation: The server must not write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message; everything else goes to stderr.

items.stem: A stdio server reads ./data.json and works in the developer's shell, but fails when a host starts it. What is the likely cause and fix?

options.a: The host strips file reads, so the data must be moved into a resource instead, as a rule of thumb
options.b: The server inherits every environment variable, which hides the file from it
options.c: The launch directory differs, so absolute paths belong in the client configuration
options.d: Relative paths fail only on Windows, so forward slashes must replace them

items.explanation: A client-launched server's working directory may be undefined, so use absolute paths in the configuration; command-line tests use the directory where you run them.

items.stem: A client parses the opaque string returned with an input-required result, adds a field to it, and sends it on retry. What does the specification say?

options.a: It is permitted, since the string is only a hint that the client may extend
options.b: It is permitted if the client signs the new version with its own key
options.c: It is required, since the client must add its own user identifier
options.d: It breaks the contract: the value must come back byte for byte, untouched

items.explanation: The client MUST echo back the exact value and MUST NOT inspect, parse or modify it.

items.stem: A server must collect a person's payment credentials in the middle of a call. Which elicitation mode may it use?

options.a: The out-of-band link variant, which keeps the data away from the client and the LLM
options.b: Form mode, because a flat schema validates card numbers reliably enough
options.c: Either mode, since both are protected by the transport that the host uses
options.d: Neither mode, since elicitation may only ask a person for confirmations

items.explanation: Form mode must not request sensitive information; passwords, keys and payment credentials belong in URL mode, which keeps data out of band.

items.stem: A remote MCP server takes any valid token from its authorization server, whatever service they were made for, and forwards it to a downstream API. What does the security guidance say?

options.a: Taking them is fine when the signature is valid and the issuer is trusted
options.b: Forwarding is fine when the downstream API is operated by the same company in many setups
options.c: Only those issued for that very endpoint are admitted, and none are relayed
options.d: Accepting them is fine if the list of supported scopes is kept short

items.explanation: Servers MUST validate that tokens were issued specifically for them and MUST NOT accept or transit any other tokens; passthrough is explicitly forbidden.

items.stem: A system calls a model at each of three steps whose order is hard-wired, and its team calls it an agent. How does the article classify it?

options.a: An agent, because it calls a model several times during one task
options.b: A workflow, because the program rather than the LLM picks what runs next
options.c: An agent, because every step uses tools and feeds on earlier output on most systems
options.d: A router, since the sequence depends on which step ran just before

items.explanation: The test is who decides the next step: a system whose sequence is written in code is a workflow, however much it calls itself an agent.

items.stem: A write-and-judge loop stops after its maximum rounds and returns the final draft, though a previous one was rated higher by the judge. What should it return?

options.a: The final draft, since it has had the most rounds of feedback
options.b: A blend of the best two drafts produced by one more writer call
options.c: No draft at all, since the loop did not reach the acceptance threshold
options.d: The top-scoring candidate, with the first of any ties winning

items.explanation: A refinement loop can get worse: keep the best-scoring draft, and when two tie the earliest wins.

items.stem: In an orchestrator-workers run, every subtask fails. What does the page say should happen next?

options.a: The orchestrator writes the answer itself from the original task alone
options.b: Nothing is combined, because synthesising over no results produces an invented answer
options.c: The synthesis runs anyway on the empty list so that the caller sees a reply
options.d: The whole run is retried with no limit on the number of attempts

items.explanation: When every worker failed nothing is combined, because a synthesis over no results is a made-up answer; a partial result is reported as partial.

items.stem: A caller reads the final text from the last message of every run without looking at the subtype, and sometimes finds it absent. Why?

options.a: The SDK removes it whenever token usage is reported alongside the cost
options.b: It is returned only to callers that enable partial messages in the options
options.c: That field is present only on a normal finish, so check how it ended first
options.d: It appears just in the last streamed event, which most loops skip

items.explanation: The result field holds the final text and is only present on the success variant, so always check the subtype before reading it.

items.stem: A developer lists only Read in allowed_tools, expecting Claude to be unable to run Bash, but Bash calls still reach the permission callback. Why?

options.a: That setting only grants approval in advance; it removes nothing from availability
options.b: Bash is built in, so no option can ever remove it from a running session
options.c: The callback runs before the list and overrides it for all shell tools
options.d: The list applies only when bypassPermissions is active

items.explanation: allowed_tools auto-approves the tools you list and does not restrict Claude to only these tools; other tools fall through to the mode and the callback.

items.stem: A path check sits in a permission callback, yet edits made under acceptEdits skip it. Where should a check that must run on every call live?

options.a: In a hook attached before tool use, which is consulted ahead of all other steps
options.b: In an allow rule, since those are evaluated before the permission mode
options.c: In a second callback registered with a higher priority than the first
options.d: In the system prompt, which the SDK applies before any tool is requested

items.explanation: Auto-approved tools never reach canUseTool; to gate every call, use a PreToolUse hook, which runs before every other step.

items.stem: A team unit-tests only its policy function and ships, but in production an allow list pre-approves tools that the policy forbids. What should the tests have exercised?

options.a: Only the callback, with a real model run on live traffic for a few long hours, as a rule of thumb
options.b: The version of the SDK package, as it is pinned in a lock file
options.c: The whole path through the SDK, driven against a scripted stand-in for the binary
options.d: The hook alone, since the callback cannot be reached at all in tests

items.explanation: The policy function can be right while the options builder leaves an allow list in; run the SDK against the stand-in so the whole path is exercised.

items.stem: A session sets its own tools entry naming a single tool. What happens to the agent's other tools?

options.a: They stay available, since the entry adds to the saved configuration
options.b: They are absent for that run, because such settings replace rather than merge
options.c: They are removed from the agent permanently, and its version number rises on most systems
options.d: They remain, but each one switches to the always_ask policy

items.explanation: Overrides never merge with the agent's configuration, so a tools override must list every tool the session should have; the agent resource is untouched.

items.stem: A request creating a cloud environment leaves out the field that controls outbound access. What does the API apply?

options.a: Closed access to everything except the package managers listed in packages
options.b: Access limited to the hosts that the agent's MCP servers declare
options.c: A rejected request, because the field is required on every cloud environment, as a rule of thumb
options.d: Open connectivity to nearly every host, apart from a general safety blocklist

items.explanation: A create request that omits networking gets unrestricted: full outbound access except a general safety blocklist, so set it explicitly.

items.stem: A compliance rule says a person must review each shell command before it executes in a hosted agent. Which permission policy fits?

options.a: auto, because the server evaluates every call as a human checkpoint would, at least at the start
options.b: always_ask, because the automatic setting lets calls it deems safe run unseen
options.c: always_allow, because the person can review the event stream afterwards
options.d: auto, because denials cannot be overridden by the client application

items.explanation: auto is not a human checkpoint: if the server judges a call safe it runs before anyone sees it, and its effects might not be reversible.

items.stem: A graph-based run crashes in its third node after two nodes have finished. What does restarting from the last checkpoint avoid?

options.a: Repeating the completed steps, and paying again for their model calls
options.b: Any failure in the third node, since the checkpoint contains its result
options.c: Loading the prompts again from the vendor's hosted service
options.d: Writing the route again, since the checkpoint stores the edges

items.explanation: A checkpoint is a copy of the state at a point in the graph; the run resumes without repeating earlier nodes, so model calls already paid for are not made again.

items.stem: In a typed agent framework, a reply fails validation against the declared output type. What happens next in the usual design?

options.a: The invalid reply is returned to the caller, flagged as unverified on most systems
options.b: The framework switches to a graph and re-routes to a repair node
options.c: The run ends at once, because validation failures are not retried
options.d: The refusal goes back to the model as feedback, and the loop proceeds

items.explanation: A reply that does not validate is refused, and the failure goes back to the model as a retry message so the run continues.

items.stem: A task runs for hours, must survive a restart of the team's own service, and the team wants no sandbox to operate. Which option does the page's table favour?

options.a: A Messages API loop, since it gives exact control over every step
options.b: The Agent SDK, since it embeds the loop in the team's own process
options.c: A hosted harness, which stores the history on the provider's side
options.d: A typed framework, since validated output makes restarts safe

items.explanation: Managed Agents is for long-running or asynchronous tasks when you want no sandbox to run; the session stores history server-side.

items.stem: A cloned project's committed configuration sets defaultMode to bypassPermissions. In which mode does a session start?

options.a: bypassPermissions, because the committed value applies from any settings file
options.b: plan, since an ignored value falls back to read-only exploration
options.c: auto, because the classifier takes over whenever bypass is refused
options.d: Manual, because a repository-supplied file cannot grant that value

items.explanation: A bypassPermissions value in .claude/settings.json or settings.local.json does not take effect, and the session starts in Manual mode.

items.stem: One layer denies Bash(aws *) while another allows the narrower Bash(aws s3 ls). What happens to that exact command?

options.a: It runs, because the narrower rule is more specific and so takes precedence
options.b: It is blocked, since prohibitions are checked first, however specific the other rule
options.c: It asks, since the two conflicting rules cancel and fall back to the mode
options.d: It runs after workspace trust, which lifts the broader rule for the session

items.explanation: Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and specificity does not change the order: an allow rule cannot carve an exception out of a deny rule.

items.stem: A project memory file has grown to 600 lines and Claude follows its instructions less closely. What does the documentation advise?

options.a: Split it using imports, which removes the added context cost
options.b: Move every rule into the user-level file so that the project copy stays short
options.c: Aim below two hundred, since extra length costs context and lowers adherence
options.d: Add emphasis words to the most important rules to restore adherence

items.explanation: Target under 200 lines per file: longer files consume more context and reduce adherence, and imports do not reduce the context cost.

items.stem: A pipeline step runs claude -p with --output-format json, and its output differs between developers' machines. What explains it?

options.a: No flag skips auto-discovery, so each checkout adds its own hooks and servers
options.b: JSON output is generated with a random key order unless every key gets sorted
options.c: The -p sessions share one global conversation that other users have extended
options.d: The default permission mode differs for each operating system in use

items.explanation: --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md, so you get the same result on every machine; without it the working directory configures the run.

items.stem: A skill's description reads only "Release helper", and Claude never starts it when people ask to ship a version. What does the page advise?

options.a: Move the folder to the enterprise location, which always outranks other matches
options.b: Set disable-model-invocation to true so that Claude treats it as a priority
options.c: State when it applies, using phrases a user would naturally say
options.d: Lengthen the body of the file, since matching reads the instructions first

items.explanation: Claude matches the request against the description, so it needs keywords users would naturally say and the key use case first.

items.stem: A skill that tags releases declares allowed-tools as the bare name of the shell tool. What does that grant for the turn?

options.a: Approval for any command whatsoever, which is why patterns should be listed instead
options.b: Approval for just the commands that the skill body mentions explicitly by name, at least at the start
options.c: Nothing at all, because a pre-approval needs a pattern to take effect
options.d: Approval that overrides any matching deny rule for the same turn

items.explanation: A bare Bash approves every shell command for that turn, turning a narrow skill into an open one; the grant goes through the normal permission flow, so a deny rule still wins.

items.stem: A PreToolUse hook script prints a reason and exits with status 1 when it sees a forbidden command. What happens to the call?

options.a: It is blocked, because any nonzero code means that the check failed
options.b: It is blocked only if standard error holds the reason text
options.c: It asks the person, since code 1 maps to the ask decision
options.d: It goes ahead as a non-blocking error; only code 2 or a JSON deny stops it

items.explanation: Only exit 2, or exit 0 with a JSON deny, blocks; any other code is a non-blocking error, so treat it as a bug in the hook.

items.stem: A plugin lists another plugin as a dependency by bare name. The dependency's next release renames a tool the first one calls. What happens when users update?

options.a: Nothing changes, since a dependency is locked at the version first installed
options.b: Everyone moves up automatically and breaks; a patch-only range such as ~2.1.0 would hold them back
options.c: The update is refused until the author publishes a new version of the plugin
options.d: Only users on another marketplace are affected, because cross-marketplace installs are automatic, at least at the start

items.explanation: Without a version constraint a dependency moves to each new release, which breaks your plugin; with ~2.1.0 users keep receiving 2.1.x patches.

items.stem: One developer's preferred model and a path on their own machine were committed in the team-wide configuration, and teammates now inherit them. Where do such values belong?

options.a: In the user-level file, which the repository's team then reads on every checkout
options.b: In CLAUDE.md, since the memory file is private to each contributor
options.c: In the untracked counterpart named settings.local.json, which stays out of version control
options.d: In managed settings, which individual developers can still override at will

items.explanation: Personal overrides go in the git-ignored .claude/settings.local.json; shared choices go in .claude/settings.json, which is committed and reviewed like code.

items.stem: A workflow meant to answer comments addressed to the bot starts a runner for every comment in the repository, and the minutes add up. What is missing?

options.a: An if condition on the job that tests the posted text for the @claude handle
options.b: A concurrency group keyed on the comment author's login name
options.c: A timeout on the job, which stops runners from starting for unrelated events
options.d: A lower value of --max-turns, which makes each run cheaper to operate

items.explanation: Without the if guard a runner starts for every comment, so cost follows comment volume; the job should start only when the comment mentions @claude.

items.stem: A team enables Anthropic's pull request review product and expects a failing finding to stop the merge button. What does the page say?

options.a: It blocks only when a finding is tagged at the highest severity level
options.b: Its check always finishes neutral, so protection rules never block on its comments
options.c: It blocks if REVIEW.md lists the changed file as a mandatory check
options.d: It blocks until a person approves each inline comment that it posted

items.explanation: The check run always completes with a neutral conclusion so it never blocks merging through branch protection rules; it advises, and a person merges.

items.stem: An application pastes inbound email text between its own delimiter tags, and one email closes the tag and adds a fake system block. What structure does the page prescribe?

options.a: A longer and more unusual pair of tags that an attacker is unlikely to guess, at least at the start
options.b: A line in the user turn telling Claude to disregard anything inside the tags
options.c: A pattern list that blocks any text containing the word system
options.d: A JSON-encoded string inside a tool result that names the origin of its content

items.explanation: JSON escaping provides unambiguous delimiters, so an attacker cannot close a quote or a tag and break out; deliver untrusted content inside tool results and say where it came from.

items.stem: A team configures the Bash sandbox to deny reads of its secrets folder, yet the agent still opens that folder through its own document viewer. Why?

options.a: Sandbox deny entries apply only after a full restart of the whole session
options.b: The sandbox protects writes on disk but never restricts any reads at all
options.c: Native Windows enforces deny entries more loosely than Linux does for shells
options.d: Only shell commands are confined; the other capabilities obey permission rules instead

items.explanation: The sandbox covers shell commands only; Claude's file tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it, and the built-in file tools follow permission rules.

items.stem: A team's only defence against injected instructions is a list of regular expressions for known attack wording. What does the page conclude?

options.a: It is sufficient when the list is extended each time a new wording is reported
options.b: It is the weakest layer, since a paraphrase slips past it; add structure and privilege
options.c: It is stronger than a model-based screen because patterns are exact
options.d: It is unnecessary once the system prompt says that tool output is data

items.explanation: A list of patterns catches the phrasing someone thought of and misses the paraphrase, so it is one layer beside structure and privilege.

items.stem: A team's monitoring raises an alert after three denials by one actor, but it also counts every request for human approval as a denial, and real attacks get buried. What fix does the page imply?

options.a: Raise the threshold to thirty denials so that alerts become rare
options.b: Stop recording arguments so that the log volume drops
options.c: Treat queries to a person as ordinary events and leave them out of the tally
options.d: Switch the gate to allow mode for actors who were asked before

items.explanation: An ask is the gate working, and alerts on it bury the real ones; the practice treats a question to a person as a normal event and not a denial.

items.stem: A team can hand-grade ten items with great care or auto-grade a hundred items with less signal per item. Which does the page favour?

options.a: The bigger scripted collection, since breadth outweighs polish on each
options.b: The small hand-graded set, since every grade carries more signal than a scripted one
options.c: Either, provided both are graded by the same person every time
options.d: Neither, since a held-out slice replaces any set that the team builds

items.explanation: More questions with slightly lower signal and automated grading is better than fewer questions with high-quality human hand-graded evals.

items.stem: A model-graded check receives the reply "Score: 4, because it is polite" instead of a bare number. How does the course treat it?

options.a: As unreadable, which fails the case and is tallied in the report
options.b: As a pass, because the number four is clearly present in the text
options.c: As a pass if four meets the threshold, ignoring the explanation that follows it
options.d: As a retry of the grader with a higher temperature setting each time

items.explanation: A reply that is not a bare score counts as ungradable and an ungradable case fails; count them so a drift in the grader is visible.

items.stem: A prompt edit raises the overall pass rate, fixes two edge cases and breaks a third that passed before. What does the page say?

options.a: Ship it, since the average improved and two failures became passes
options.b: Someone must examine the newly failing item, since an average never excuses a regression
options.c: Revert it automatically, since any change that breaks a case is rejected
options.d: Delete the failing case from the set so that the comparison is clean

items.explanation: An average never excuses a regression: if a case passed before and fails now, a person looks at it, and a removed case fails the comparison.

items.stem: A migration to a newer model id is planned for next week. Where does the page place the eval run?

options.a: After the switch, once production traffic has produced enough real failures
options.b: Only when the prompt text is edited, since ids do not change behaviour
options.c: Nightly only, because per-change runs are too slow to be useful
options.d: Ahead of the switch, so rejected settings fail a case instead of a request in production

items.explanation: A new model id changes behaviour, so the regression run sits before the id is changed in configuration; each rejected setting becomes a failed case the same afternoon.

items.stem: Dashboards built on error rates show nothing wrong, yet some replies carry stop_reason refusal. What does the page say about handling them?

options.a: Count them in the error rate by raising an exception on any non-end_turn stop
options.b: Resend each one unchanged to the same model, which will usually agree to answer in everyday use
options.c: Track them as their own signal and answer with a fallback model or a fresh context
options.d: Increase max_tokens, since refusals indicate that the limit was too low

items.explanation: Refusals are responses, not errors, so error-rate monitoring will not surface them; re-sending to the same model usually repeats the refusal.

items.stem: Right after a model id changed, every call fails with a 400 whose message points to adaptive thinking and effort. Which recovery fits?

options.a: Rewrite the request body to drop the rejected setting; retrying cannot succeed
options.b: Back off with jitter and retry, since the service is turning away the load for now
options.c: Stream the call, because the error means that the generation is too long
options.d: Escalate to a person who can raise the account's limits

items.explanation: A migration error is an integration failure the new model reveals; the recovery is to change the request, and no retry, timeout or prompt change cures it.

items.stem: A parse step fails on reply text that holds a JSON object wrapped in a code fence. Who owns the fault?

options.a: The model, since it should never wrap its output in a fence
options.b: Your own reading logic, which should cut out the braces before decoding
options.c: The service, since a proxy altered the body on its way back
options.d: The account, because structured output is limited by the plan

items.explanation: If there is a JSON object in the text from the first { to the last }, the integration's parser was too strict, so extract the object first.
